opus-5.5.text:
I think the next stage is really about adapting to how much the landscape has changed. When we started TVM, the core question was how to take models from frameworks and run them efficiently across very diverse hardware: CPUs, GPUs, mobile chips, accelerators. That problem hasn't gone away, but the workloads have shifted dramatically. Today a lot of the attention is on large language models and generative AI, which bring their own challenges: dynamic shapes, huge memory pressure, KV-cache management, and the need to combine compiler optimizations with runtime systems.

So one big direction for us has been rethinking the abstractions. Through efforts like the Unity work and Relax, we've moved toward a design where the compiler isn't a closed, one-shot pipeline. Instead, it's something you can program and compose. You can bring in hand-written kernels, vendor libraries, or code generated by other tools, and mix them with automatically optimized code in the same flow. I think that's essential, because in practice nobody wins by being purely automatic or purely manual. The real value comes from letting engineers and the compiler collaborate.

Another direction is making machine-learning compilation more accessible and more Pythonic, so that ML engineers, not just compiler experts, can customize and iterate quickly. Projects like MLC LLM, where we bring large models to run natively on phones, browsers through WebGPU, and all kinds of GPUs, are a good example of what that enables. They also serve as a kind of forcing function, pushing the core infrastructure to be more flexible.

Longer term, I see the field converging on an ecosystem view. There will be many compilers, many kernel languages, and many hardware backends, and the important thing is interoperability. I'd like TVM to be a foundation that helps people bring new hardware and new models together quickly, and to keep it an open, community-driven project where researchers and industry can experiment together. That has always been the spirit of it, and I think that's what will keep it relevant.

r001.rationale: The response discusses flexible compiler abstractions and interoperability across compilers and hardware, but does not identify rapidly building compilers for specific vertical domains as a direction.

r002.rationale: It mentions interoperability generally, but does not propose abstracting shared function-call conventions or name PyTorch and JAX.

r003.rationale: It calls for more accessible, Pythonic compilation, but does not say deep-learning compilation should be as easy as writing a neural network.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that TVM has to keep evolving, because the problems have changed a lot since we started.

When we began, the central question was pretty clear: you have a static computation graph, you want to run it on some piece of hardware, and you want the compiler to generate code that's as good as or better than hand-tuned libraries. A lot of the early work, like the tensor expression language and auto-tuning with AutoTVM and later Ansor, was really about that. And that mattered, because it let one codebase target CPUs, GPUs, mobile chips, accelerators, without a vendor having to write a kernel library from scratch.

But the landscape now is dominated by large language models, and that changes a few things. The workloads are more dynamic, you have variable sequence lengths, KV caches that grow, batching decisions that happen at runtime. You also have a lot more interaction between the model, the runtime system, and the hardware. So the next stage, in my view, is less about "compile one graph as fast as possible" and more about building a unified abstraction where graph-level transformations, tensor-level kernels, and runtime behavior all live in the same framework and can be optimized together. That's a lot of what Relax and TVM Unity are about: letting you write the high-level program, the low-level kernels, and the dynamic shape logic in one place, and letting Python be the first-class interface for all of it.

The other shift is in who the user is. Early on, our users were mostly compiler people. Now I think the most interesting users are machine-learning engineers who want to deploy a model on their laptop, their phone, or a web browser, and they want that to be a weekend project, not a research agenda. Projects like MLC LLM and WebLLM really grew out of that. If a compiler framework can get a model running efficiently on an iPhone or in WebGPU with minimal manual effort, that's a sign the infrastructure is doing its job.

So if I had to summarize: the next stage is about universal deployment, dynamic workloads, and making the whole stack programmable and composable, rather than picking any one layer to optimize in isolation. And doing it in the open, because the hardware ecosystem is only getting more diverse, and no single company can cover all of it on its own.

r001.rationale: The response discusses universal deployment and a unified framework, but does not identify rapidly building compilers for specific vertical domains as a development direction.

r002.rationale: It does not propose abstracting shared function-call conventions or mention interoperability between PyTorch and JAX.

r003.rationale: It describes making model deployment easier and Python a first-class interface, but does not state that deep-learning compilation should be as easy as writing a neural network.

astra-6.text:
I think the next stage is about making TVM more useful as an end-to-end machine-learning compilation system. Optimizing an individual operator is important, but we also need to think about how the whole model runs, how it interacts with the runtime, and how developers can bring it to different hardware platforms.

There’s an interesting balance here. We want to automate more of the optimization work, while still giving hardware experts a way to express their knowledge and control the parts that matter. A good compiler infrastructure should support both.

And I think the community is central to that development. Different people bring different models, hardware, and deployment requirements. The opportunity is to turn what we learn from those use cases into reusable infrastructure, so that supporting the next model or the next device becomes easier.

r002.rationale: It does not mention abstracting shared function-call conventions or interoperability between frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX.

r003.rationale: It does not state that deep-learning compilation should be as easy as writing a neural network.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next stage is to make TVM easier to use while continuing to support a broader range of models and hardware. A machine-learning compiler should help people take a model they care about and deploy it efficiently, without requiring them to understand every detail of the underlying system.

That means improving the whole path, from bringing a model into TVM to optimizing it, running it, and understanding its performance. We also need to make it easier for hardware developers to bring new devices into that workflow.

For me, the community is central to this. There are many different workloads and hardware platforms, and no single team can anticipate all of them. The opportunity is to build shared infrastructure that lets researchers and engineers contribute new ideas, while making those ideas useful to people deploying real applications.

r001.rationale: The response calls for making TVM easier to use and supporting more models and hardware, but does not identify rapidly constructing compilers for specific vertical domains.

r002.rationale: It mentions bringing models into TVM and integrating new hardware, but does not propose abstracting shared function-call conventions for interoperability between frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX.

r003.rationale: The response says TVM should be easier to use, but does not state that deep-learning compilation should be as easy as writing a neural network.
